title: Mini Chess Board
story: Sixty-four squares. Thirty-two pieces. Infinite possibilities. Chess is the king of strategy games, played for over 1500 years. Today you build the board — an 8x8 grid with pieces in their starting positions. White pawns in a row. Rooks in the corners. The royal court: King and Queen at center. Display it as a beautiful text board. Then go further: select any pawn and the engine shows where it can legally move. You've just written the visualization layer of a chess engine.
why: Chess board construction teaches 2D grid modeling with Vec of Vec, enums for piece types and colors, positioning logic with coordinates, match expression dispatch for display, and basic movement rule implementation — a foundation for game AI.
analogy: A physical chessboard set up on a table. Each piece has its designated starting square — white pieces on rows 1 and 2, black on rows 7 and 8. Rooks in corners like castle towers, knights next to them (the horses), bishops, then royalty in the center. The coordinate system is like a spreadsheet: columns are files (a-h), rows are ranks (1-8). Pawn movement rules: forward one square, or two from starting position. Captures are diagonal — but that's for another lesson.
try_it: Add knight movement: from a given position, generate all 8 L-shaped moves (2+1 or 1+2) that stay on the board. Add piece color (White/Black) to distinguish sides — uppercase for white, lowercase for black. Add a 'move' function that moves a piece from one square to another, clearing the source. Display legal pawn moves when a pawn is 'selected.'
tips: White pieces are uppercase (K, Q, R, B, N, P), black lowercase (k, q, r, b, n, p) — standard notation
Rows 0-7 in code = ranks 8-1 on display — reverse the row order when printing for correct orientation
Back rank order (from left/a-file): Rook, Knight, Bishop, Queen, King, Bishop, Knight, Rook — symmetrical
common_mistakes: Black pieces on rows 0-1 and white on 6-7 — not rows 7-8 vs 1-2 when printing (displays inverted)
Column labels (a-h) correspond to indices 0-7 — 'a1' is grid[7][0], not grid[0][0]
Forgetting that pawns move forward only — direction depends on color: white moves up (decreasing row), black moves down (increasing row)
